newsitem.title: USA: Kellogg sees rising sales of convenience food.
newsitem.headline: Kellogg sees rising sales of convenience food.

text.p: Kellogg Co, the world's largest cereal maker, on Friday said it expected convenience foods to contribute a larger percentage of its annual sales in coming years.

Currently about 20 percent of Kellogg's $6.68 billion in annual sales comes from convenience foods such as Pop-Tarts and Nutri-Grain bars. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Arnold Langbo said that figure could rise to 30 percent in 10 years as the company expands in the United States and elsewhere.

Langbo, at a news briefing after the company's annual meeting in Battle Creek, said Kellogg was rolling out convenience foods around the world. At the same time the category is growing in North America at about 10 percent a year, he said.
"It would be my expectation that convenience will be a larger percentage of Kellogg going forward, perhaps even as high as 30 percent over the next 10 years," he said.

Despite the popularity of restaurants that sell fresh bagels, Langbo said Kellogg sees big growth opportunities for Lender's Bagels, although he said the category needs additional marketing and innovation.

Specifically, Kellogg sees "excellent opportunities" for getting an early start into international frozen bagel markets, Langbo said. For instance, he said there are no frozen bagels sold in supermarkets in Canada.
Kellogg purchased Lender's last December for $455 million in its largest acquisition ever. Lenders controls 80 percent of the U.S. frozen bagel segment.
To be sure, ready-to-eat cereal will remain the dominant segment of Kellogg's business, Langbo said. Worldwide, cereal is the fastest-growing large category in food stores, he said.
For Kellogg, Langbo said the company aimed to at least match the U.S. industry volume growth of about 2 percent and international cereal growth of about 5 percent.
In contrast with last year, when Kellogg slashed prices on two-thirds of its U.S. cereals by 19 percent, Lanbgo said the company had no plans for any broad-based price reductions.

Langbo said Kellogg sought to increase its share of the U.S. cereal market this year with the introduction of new products such as Cocoa Frosted Flakes and better marketing. He declined to provide specific projections.

For the four weeks ended April 6, Kellogg had 35.4 percent of the U.S. market. That is about 10 percentage points more than its nearest competitor, and up from its low point of 31 percent in the autumn of 1996, during last year's pricing wars.
